section.title: Eliphaz's First Speech
section.sectionRationale: Eliphaz breaks the seven days of silence and opens the first of three cycles of dialogue. He is the gentlest of the friends, appealing to Job's own past wisdom, a mystical night vision, and genuinely true statements about human sinfulness and divine discipline. But his underlying principle, that suffering proves sin and prosperity proves righteousness, will be applied to Job with increasing cruelty by the friends as the book goes on, and it is this very principle that God will rebuke at the book's end.
section.thesis: Eliphaz's first speech mixes real wisdom, that no mortal is pure before God and that God's discipline of His people is good, with a rigid principle applied wrongly to Job: that his suffering must be traced to some fault, when the reader already knows it was not.
section.frameNote: Six movements: Eliphaz's gentle opening appeal to Job's own past counsel; his stated principle that the innocent do not perish; a night vision revealing that no mortal is pure before God; his observation that man is born to trouble; his counsel to appeal to God, who does great and unsearchable things; and his closing promise that the man God corrects will be restored.

units.label: A gentle beginning
units.note: your words have steadied those who stumbled

verses.text: Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied:
"If one ventures a word with you, will you be wearied? Yet who can keep from speaking?
Surely you have instructed many, and have strengthened their feeble hands.
Your words have steadied those who stumbled; you have braced the knees that were buckling.
But now trouble has come upon you, and you are weary. It strikes you, and you are dismayed.
Is your reverence not your confidence, and the {{yosher|uprightness}} of your ways your hope?

units.label: Who, being innocent, has perished?
units.note: those who plow iniquity reap the same

verses.text:
Consider now, I plead: 
Who, being innocent, has ever perished? Or where have the upright been destroyed?
As I have observed, those who plow iniquity and those who sow trouble reap the same.
By the breath of {{eloah|God}} they perish, and by the blast of His anger they are consumed.
The lion may roar, and the fierce lion may growl, yet the teeth of the young lions are broken.
The old lion perishes for lack of prey, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered.

units.label: A vision in the night
units.note: can a mortal be more righteous than God

verses.text: Now a word came to me secretly; my ears caught a whisper of it.
In disquieting visions in the night, when deep sleep falls on men,
fear and trembling came over me and made all my bones shudder.
Then a spirit glided past my face, and the hair on my body bristled.
It stood still, but I could not discern its appearance; a form loomed before my eyes, and I heard a whispering voice:
'Can a mortal be more righteous than God, or a man more pure than his Maker?
If God puts no trust in His servants, and He charges His angels with error,

how much more those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundations are in the dust, 
who can be crushed like a moth!
They are smashed to pieces from dawn to dusk; unnoticed, they perish forever.
Are not their tent cords pulled up, so that they die without wisdom?'

units.label: Man is born to trouble
units.note: as surely as sparks fly upward

verses.text: "Call out if you please, but who will answer? To which of the holy ones will you turn?
For resentment kills a fool, and envy slays the simple.
I have seen a fool taking root, but suddenly his house was cursed.
His sons are far from safety, crushed in court without a defender.

The hungry consume his harvest, taking it even from the thorns, 
and the thirsty pant after his wealth.
For distress does not spring from the dust, and trouble does not sprout from the ground.
Yet man is born to trouble as surely as sparks fly upward.

units.label: Appeal to God, who does great things

verses.text: However, if I were you, I would appeal to God and lay my cause before Him,
the One who does great and unsearchable things, wonders without number.
He gives rain to the earth and sends water upon the fields.
He sets the lowly on high, so that mourners are lifted to safety.
He thwarts the schemes of the crafty, so that their hands find no success.
He catches the wise in their craftiness, and sweeps away the plans of the cunning.
They encounter darkness by day and grope at noon as in the night.
He saves the needy from the sword in their mouth and from the clutches of the powerful.
So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts its mouth.

units.label: Blessed is the man whom God corrects
units.note: He wounds, but He also binds

verses.text: Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects; so do not despise the {{musar|discipline}} of the {{shadday|Almighty}}.
For He wounds, but He also binds; He strikes, but His hands also heal.
He will rescue you from six calamities; no harm will touch you in seven.
In famine He will redeem you from death, and in battle from the stroke of the sword.
You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, and will not fear havoc when it comes.
You will laugh at destruction and famine, and need not fear the beasts of the earth.
For you will have a covenant with the stones of the field, and the wild animals will be at peace with you.
You will know that your tent is secure, and find nothing amiss when inspecting your home.
You will know that your offspring will be many, your descendants like the grass of the earth.
You will come to the grave in full vigor, like a sheaf of grain gathered in season.
Indeed, we have investigated, and it is true! So hear it and know for yourself."

yosher.gloss: Uprightness, straightness of conduct. Eliphaz appeals to it as the ground of Job's hope, assuming that Job's own uprightness should now be enough to secure his deliverance, an assumption the rest of the book will complicate rather than confirm.

eloah.gloss: God, a poetic singular form used far more often in Job than anywhere else in the Old Testament, favored in this book's elevated speech instead of the covenant name YHWH. Its frequent use across all the speeches, friends and Job alike, marks Job as addressing the God of all humanity, not only the God of Israel's covenant history.

musar.gloss: Discipline, correction, moral instruction, the same word that anchors much of the book of Proverbs. Eliphaz's claim that Job's suffering is God's musar assumes it functions as fatherly correction for sin; whether that assumption fits Job's actual case is exactly what the book contests.

shadday.gloss: The Almighty, a name for God used with striking frequency throughout Job, emphasizing overwhelming power. Both Job and his friends use this name freely; the dispute in the book is never over whether God is almighty, but over how that almighty power relates to human suffering.

basic.context: Eliphaz speaks first among the friends, and gently. He reminds Job that Job himself has comforted others in trouble before, then states his core conviction: the innocent do not perish, and those who sow trouble reap it. He backs this up with a mysterious night vision in which a spirit tells him no mortal can be pure before God. He observes that man is born to trouble as sparks fly upward, but counsels Job to appeal to God, who does wondrous things and lifts up the lowly. He closes with a genuinely beautiful promise: that the one God disciplines will be restored, protected, and blessed with long life.
basic.hermeneutics: Much of what Eliphaz says here is true in general and even quotable, no mortal is pure before God, God's discipline of His own is good, God does wondrous things for the humble. The error is not in these general truths but in the specific application: Eliphaz assumes Job's catastrophic suffering must be correction for some fault, when the reader already knows from chapters 1 and 2 that it is not. This is the book's first demonstration that true words, wrongly applied to a particular sufferer, can wound rather than heal.
basic.originalLanguages: Eliphaz uses eloah and shadday, poetic and powerful names for God favored throughout this book, and appeals to Job's yosher, uprightness, as though it alone should secure deliverance. His counsel that Job's suffering is God's musar, discipline, assumes a direct link between suffering and correction for fault, the very link the whole book will complicate.
basic.typology: Eliphaz's true but misapplied words anticipate the danger of proof-texting suffering, applying real biblical truths carelessly to specific people in pain, a temptation the church has faced in every generation since. His promise of restoration after discipline, though wrongly timed for Job, does anticipate the true pattern of discipline and restoration God brings to His children in Christ.
basic.christ: Eliphaz's vision declares that no mortal is pure before God, not even His angels; the whole book will eventually show that no human wisdom, however sincere, is sufficient to explain suffering rightly. Only Christ, truly righteous and yet willingly afflicted though guiltless, breaks the assumed link between suffering and personal fault that Eliphaz cannot see past. Where Eliphaz promises the disciplined will be restored to prosperity, Christ promises something greater: resurrection life for all who are united to Him, whether or not restoration comes in this life.
basic.god: Eliphaz's God is real and rightly described in many particulars: powerful, just, the one who lifts the lowly and disciplines those He loves. But Eliphaz's God is also too small in this speech, boxed into a formula that cannot account for Job's actual situation, a warning about how easily true doctrine can be twisted into a rigid system.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 12:5-11 affirms that God does discipline those He loves, while also insisting no discipline seems pleasant at the time; Romans 3:10 echoes the vision's claim that none is righteous, no not one; John 9:2-3 shows Jesus explicitly rejecting the assumption that suffering always traces to sin.
basic.oneStory: Eliphaz opens the dialogue with words that sound wise and often are, yet applied wrongly to an innocent sufferer they become part of the very failure God will rebuke at the book's end. His speech teaches the church to handle true doctrine carefully, since even sound words can wound when spoken without knowledge of the actual case before us.

context.literary:
Eliphaz's speech is the best-made speech among the friends, and it is built in four panels. The first, Job 4:2 to 4:11, opens with a courteous hesitation and turns Job's own past into an argument, then states the thesis in a question, 'Who, being innocent, has ever perished?' and backs it with farm and lion imagery. The second, Job 4:12 to 4:21, is the night vision, the only place in the book where a friend claims direct revelation. The third, Job 5:1 to 5:16, moves from warning about the fool to counsel: 'I would appeal to God,' Job 5:8, followed by a hymn of God's wonders. The fourth, Job 5:17 to 5:27, is a blessing on the disciplined man and a set of promises, closed by a claim to have checked it all.

The poet uses devices with care. Job 4:10-11 lists five different Hebrew words for lions, a rich stack of images for the powerful who are broken. Job 5:19 uses a graded numerical saying, 'six calamities... in seven,' a form found also in the wisdom sayings of Proverbs. The whole discourse is also framed by the word amal, trouble or toil: the sowers of trouble reap it, Job 4:8, trouble does not spring from the ground, Job 5:6, and man is born to it, Job 5:7.

The speech is not a cold argument. It begins in tenderness, with Job's record as a comforter of others, Job 4:3-4, and it ends with a gentle picture of old age like a sheaf gathered in season, Job 5:26. Its warmth is what makes it dangerous. It is a single beautiful piece of reasoning that keeps returning to one point: Job's suffering must mean something about Job.

In the book's larger plan this is the first speech of the whole dialogue. Eliphaz speaks first and gentlest, and his opening frames everything after. If Job's later answers seem sharp, this is what they answer.
context.historical:
Eliphaz the Temanite comes from Teman, an Edomite region associated with wisdom. Jeremiah 49:7 asks, 'Is there no longer wisdom in Teman?' and Genesis 36:11 names a Teman among the sons of Eliphaz in Esau's line. A man of Teman in a story set among the patriarchs would have been received as one of the East's wise elders, and his speech is built from what such elders offered: inherited proverb, careful observation and, in Job 4:12-16, a night experience.

Wisdom in the ancient Near East was practical and confident. A person who lived rightly could expect a good life, and misfortune was often read as a sign of a hidden fault. Egyptian and Mesopotamian wisdom writings contain sufferers' complaints and the conviction that the gods reward and punish, and Israel's own Proverbs holds that the righteous are rewarded, Proverbs 22:8 and Galatians 6:7. Eliphaz speaks from inside that moral universe. What Job's story shows is that the tradition he speaks from was never meant to be used as a universal key to a single person's pain.

The imagery of the lion, the sowing and reaping, the tent cord pulled up and the covenant with the stones of the field draws on the pastoral and agricultural world of the patriarchal age. The farmer who ploughs iniquity reaps it, and stones in the field that once threatened the plough become friends, Job 5:23.

The night vision, Job 4:12-21, has a real cultural home: revelation was expected to come by dreams and visions when 'deep sleep falls on men,' and Elihu uses the same phrase of God's warning speech, Job 33:14-18. The difference is that Eliphaz uses the vision as authority over another man's case, and no one in the book verifies it.
context.canonical:
Job 4 and 5 are the passages of Job most often quoted, so their canonical afterlife is unusually rich. Paul quotes Job 5:13 in 1 Corinthians 3:19: 'He catches the wise in their craftiness.' Scripture here uses a line from a speech that God will later say did not speak of Him accurately, Job 42:7, and the BSB footnote at Job 5:13 marks it. The New Testament can quote a true sentence from a mistaken speaker without endorsing the speaker.

The principle behind Job 4:8, that people reap what they sow, is at home in Proverbs 22:8, Hosea 10:13 and Galatians 6:7-8. Eliphaz cites a real biblical pattern. Job 5:17-18, 'Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects... For He wounds, but He also binds,' has close kin in Deuteronomy 32:39, 'I wound and I heal,' in Hosea 6:1, 'He has wounded us, but He will bind up our wounds,' and in Proverbs 3:11-12, which the letter to the Hebrews quotes to encourage suffering believers, Hebrews 12:5-6.

But the canon also limits Eliphaz. The book of Job itself corrects him in the same narrative. Job 9:10 repeats Eliphaz's words about God's wonders, 'He does great things beyond searching out, and wonders without number,' now as an argument that God cannot be summoned to a court. The book of Ecclesiastes says that the righteous sometimes perish, Ecclesiastes 7:15, and the Psalms often ask why the wicked prosper. The Gospels supply the final correction when Jesus refuses to read a tragedy as a verdict on its victims, Luke 13:1-5, and above all in His own case, for the innocent One perished.

The vision of Job 4:17 recurs in Job 15:14-16 and Job 25:4 as a favourite of the friends, and Paul's teaching that no one is justified by works, Romans 3:20, gives the truth in it a new footing: none is righteous before God, and the answer is a righteousness from God, received by faith.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wanted hearers to feel how good this counsel sounds. Eliphaz is gentle, respectful and full of true theology. The hearer is invited to nod along, and then is made to see, from the prologue's knowledge, that the whole speech is aimed at the wrong man. The book is teaching a skill: to hear a wise voice without letting it explain a person who has not been heard.

The speech also shows the author's concern with the sources of religious authority. Eliphaz appeals to observation, 'as I have observed,' Job 4:8, to a private revelation, Job 4:12-16, and to a joint investigation, 'we have investigated, and it is true,' Job 5:27. Each is a real way of knowing in Israel. The author places them side by side to show that none of them, alone or together, gives access to the reason for one man's suffering. Only God's own word settles that, and the reader already has it in Job 1 and 2.

Finally the speech is meant to test how hearers treat a sufferer. Eliphaz's first words, 'If one ventures a word with you, will you be wearied?' Job 4:2, show that he has thought about how to approach Job, and yet he goes on to tell Job what his pain means. The hearer is asked whether the same could be said of them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Eliphaz's speech is recorded, not commended. Scripture reports faithfully what he said, and it does not make his applications a rule. Job 42:7 makes it plain that the friends did not speak rightly of God, and this speech is where the book begins to show why.

That does not make every sentence in it false. Several lines are true and are taken up elsewhere in the Bible. God does discipline those He loves, Hebrews 12:5-6, He does bind up what He wounds, Hosea 6:1, and He does lift the lowly, Job 5:11. So the right way to use this passage is to test each line against the rest of Scripture and not to accept or reject it as a package.

The passage also teaches by counter-example. It warns counsellors against three habits: quoting a principle at a person in pain, appealing to a private experience as if it were an argument, and closing with 'we have investigated, and it is true' about matters God has not explained. Those who visit the sick and grieving should do as Eliphaz did in Job 4:3-4, remembering the person's past faithfulness, and should stop where he went on. The passage does not tell us to rebuke all comfort; it tells us to test our comfort against what we actually know.

debates.question: How can Eliphaz's speech contain real truths yet still be wrong?

views.label: The truths are wrongly applied to Job's specific case
views.case: Statements like 'no mortal is pure before God' and 'God disciplines those He loves' are sound in general. His error is applying them to conclude that Job's suffering proves some fault, which the reader knows is false from Job 1:8 and Job 2:3.

views.label: The truths themselves are incomplete, needing the fuller picture the book will supply
views.case: Even taken generally, Eliphaz's principle that the innocent never perish, Job 4:7, is too absolute. The rest of Scripture and Job's own life show innocent suffering is real, so his framework needs correcting, not only his application of it.

debates.bearing: Either way, the chapter warns readers against treating any general spiritual principle, however true it sounds, as an infallible explanation for a specific person's suffering.

debates.question: What is the source and meaning of the night vision in Job 4:12-21?

views.label: A genuine spirit or messenger, with a true message wrongly applied
views.case: The vision has the marks of real revelation: night, deep sleep, dread, a form that stands still. Its content is orthodox, that no one is pure before his Maker. On this view God permitted the vision, but Eliphaz mis-hears what it was for. Elihu describes God warning in dreams in Job 33:14-18.

views.label: A misleading or untested experience
views.case: The spirit is never identified, its form 'could not be discerned,' and the BSB footnote notes it could be 'a wind.' Scripture tells believers to 'test the spirits,' 1 John 4:1, and warns that Satan disguises himself as an angel of light, 2 Corinthians 11:14. Eliphaz uses the experience as authority without testing it.

views.label: Literary device that conveys the friends' view of human frailty
views.case: Some see the vision as the poet's way of dramatising the friends' theology of human sinfulness, so that its truth or falsity is less important than what it shows about how the friends argue. The vision is later echoed in the mouths of Bildad and Eliphaz, Job 15:14-16 and Job 25:4.

debates.bearing: The text does not tell us where the voice came from. Its content is orthodox, its use is wrong, and the chapter teaches that a striking experience is not the same as a word about someone else's case.

debates.question: Does 'more righteous than God' in Job 4:17 mean what the BSB says?

views.label: Comparative: can a mortal be more righteous than his Maker
views.case: The Hebrew preposition min can be comparative, and the parallel line, 'more pure than his Maker,' repeats the comparison. On this reading the question is absurd on its face and the answer is no, so no one has grounds to complain about God.

views.label: Before God: can a mortal be righteous in the sight of God
views.case: The same preposition can mean 'from the standpoint of' or 'before,' so that the question is whether anyone is in the right before God. This is the sense of many translations, and it connects to Job 25:4 and Psalm 143:2. It makes the thesis a doctrine of universal guilt.

debates.bearing: Both readings lead to the same verdict about human frailty. The difference is in the tone of the argument: whether the vision warns against arrogance against God or against any claim to be clean before Him.

study.originalLanguages:
Eliphaz's opening argument in Job 4:6 turns God's own words into a syllogism. He says, 'Is your reverence not your confidence, and the uprightness of your ways your hope?' The Hebrew for 'uprightness' is tom, from the root that gives tam and tummah, the 'blameless' and 'integrity' of Job 1:1 and Job 2:3. God said Job is tam, and Eliphaz says the tom of your ways should be your hope. He is quoting Job's good name back to him and drawing the wrong conclusion. His word for 'reverence,' yirah, comes from the same root as the verb in Satan's question, 'Does Job fear God for nothing?' Job 1:9.

In Job 4:7 the word for 'innocent' is naqi, clean or free of guilt, the same word used in the law for the innocent who must not be put to death, Exodus 23:7. The verb 'perished' is avad, the word Job used in Job 3:3 for the day to perish. The overlap is not accidental. Eliphaz picks up the verb Job used and asks who has ever perished innocent, and the question is made to answer Job's grief.

The five words for lion in Job 4:10-11, aryeh, shachal, kefir, layish and lavi, are a display of eloquence and of the theme. However fierce the lion, it is broken. The proverb of the powerful who are destroyed is used against Job, who has been a powerful man, Job 1:3.

In Job 4:9 the wicked perish 'by the breath of God,' nishmat Eloah, the word for breath used in Genesis 2:7 when God breathed into man. The same breath that gives life takes it away. Then the voice in Job 4:16 is described as demamah vakol, literally 'a stillness and a voice,' which the BSB renders as 'a whispering voice.' The idiom captures the hush before the sound. The 'spirit' of Job 4:15 is ruach, the ordinary word for wind or spirit, and the BSB footnote notes that it can be 'a wind.'

In Job 5:2, kaas is 'resentment' and qin'ah is 'envy,' and the word kaas will be picked up by Job in the next chapter when he asks that his own kaas be weighed. In Job 5:7, 'sparks' is literally 'sons of reshef,' where reshef can mean flame or fiery bolt. Some old translators took it as a bird of prey, and either way it means things that fly up as certainly as trouble comes to man. The trouble is amal, the same word Eliphaz used for the trouble sown and reaped in Job 4:8.

Job 5:13, 'He catches the wise in their craftiness,' uses the noun ormah, from the same root as the word for the serpent in Genesis 3:1, arum. The craft that can be wisdom in Proverbs is, when turned against God, a snare.

Then the closing words. In Job 5:9 God's works are 'unsearchable,' literally 'there is no cheqer,' no searching out. In Job 5:27 Eliphaz says, 'we have investigated,' chaqarnuha, from the same root. The speech ends by claiming to have searched what it earlier said cannot be searched. Job will bring up the same line in Job 9:10.

Finally, in Job 5:17 the word for the disciplined man's blessing is ashre, the opening word of Psalm 1, and the verb 'corrects' is yakach, to reprove or argue a case. God is pictured as the one who argues a case with a man, and Job will spend the book asking to argue his.

typology.type: 'Who, being innocent, has ever perished?' Job 4:7
typology.fulfillment: Eliphaz's rhetorical question assumes the answer is no one. The Gospels answer with a name. Pilate found no basis for the charges, Luke 23:14, Judas said he had betrayed 'innocent blood,' Matthew 27:4, and the centurion said, 'Surely this was a righteous man,' Luke 23:47. Peter tells the crowd, 'You killed the Author of life,' Acts 3:14-15. The type here is a negative one: a human generalisation that God overturns in one life. The escalation is that the Innocent One perished so that the guilty would not, Isaiah 53:9-10. The correspondence falls short as a type of Job, who was not innocent in the absolute sense.

Eliphaz says human beings dwell in 'houses of clay, whose foundations are in the dust.' The same figure returns when Paul says that believers have this treasure in 'jars of clay,' 2 Corinthians 4:7, and again when the Son takes on the same flesh, Hebrews 2:14. Eliphaz uses the image to humble; Paul uses it to show that the power is God's. The correspondence deepens because in Christ the frailty is entered by God Himself, and His people are carried through it by resurrection life. The type stops where the clay in Eliphaz's mouth is a reason for fear, and in Paul's a place where grace shows.

typology.type: 'To which of the holy ones will you turn?' Job 5:1
typology.fulfillment: Eliphaz tells Job that no angel will answer him. Job himself will later say there is no mediator between them, Job 9:32-33, and long for a witness and advocate on high, Job 16:19-21. The letter to the Hebrews says that the Son is 'far superior to the angels,' Hebrews 1:4, and Paul says, 'there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,' 1 Timothy 2:5. What Eliphaz calls a dead end becomes a door. The type falls short in that Eliphaz's question is used to silence, and Christ's answer is to invite.

typology.type: He wounds but He binds, Job 5:18
typology.fulfillment: Eliphaz states the pattern of a God who strikes and heals as a principle for Job's case. In Christ the pattern is worked out on Himself. The servant was 'pierced for our transgressions,' and 'by His stripes we are healed,' Isaiah 53:5, and Jesus takes up Isaiah 61 as His own mission, Luke 4:18-21, and its opening verse speaks of one sent 'to bind up the brokenhearted,' Isaiah 61:1. The escalation is that the wound falls not on the sufferer who needs healing but on the One who heals. The type falls short where Eliphaz makes the wound Job's correction, and the gospel makes it a substitute.

study.christ:
Job 4 and 5 lead to Christ mostly by contradiction. Eliphaz says that no one innocent perishes and that the sufferer should look to his own sin. The gospel is the story of the Innocent One who perished and of a God who did not turn away from the guilty but bore their guilt. Eliphaz's argument is the mirror image of the cross.

It leads to Christ by the question of righteousness. The night voice asks, 'Can a mortal be more righteous than God, or a man more pure than his Maker?' Job 4:17. If God does not trust His servants and finds error in His angels, Job 4:18, what hope is there for a man of clay? The Old Testament raises the question and the New Testament answers it. Paul says that 'no one will be justified in His sight by works of the law,' and that a righteousness from God 'comes through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe,' Romans 3:20-22. Peter says that Christ suffered 'the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God,' 1 Peter 3:18. Eliphaz leaves man in the dust; the gospel takes a man out of it, not by making him pure by effort but by giving him a purity that is not his own.

It leads to Christ by the theme of discipline. Job 5:17 says, 'Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects; so do not despise the discipline of the Almighty.' The author of Hebrews quotes the same wisdom from Proverbs 3 to comfort persecuted believers, Hebrews 12:5-6. But the same letter says of Jesus that 'He learned obedience from what He suffered,' Hebrews 5:8. That is a different kind of discipline, not correction for fault but the road of a Son who was without sin. Job sits between the two. His suffering is not punishment, and yet it will teach him, and the book leaves room for both truths, though not for Eliphaz's neat identification of them.

It leads to Christ by the promise of healing. 'He wounds, but He also binds; He strikes, but His hands also heal,' Job 5:18. Jesus takes up Isaiah 61, whose opening verse speaks of one sent 'to bind up the brokenhearted,' Isaiah 61:1, and says in Nazareth that it is fulfilled today, Luke 4:21. The woundings He heals are not only the ones inflicted by God's discipline but those of a world broken by sin, and the blood that heals is His own.

It leads to Christ by the promise that man is born to trouble. Job 5:7 says trouble is as sure as sparks flying upward, and that is a true remark. Jesus does not deny it: 'In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world!' John 16:33. What Eliphaz sees as the whole horizon, Christ sees as ground already crossed.

A caution: Eliphaz is not a prophet of Christ. His lines are true or false on their own merits, and the New Testament quotes or corrects them as it sees fit. The links above depend on the New Testament's own claims, especially about innocent suffering, mediation and the binding of wounds, and not on finding Jesus in Eliphaz's imagery. What this passage offers is a picture of a world in which a confident wisdom cannot reach the sufferer, and the Christ who can.
study.god:
Eliphaz says many true things about God, and this passage shows what they are. He speaks of the God who does 'great and unsearchable things, wonders without number,' Job 5:9. That is the God of creation and providence, who gives rain to the earth, Job 5:10. He is the God who acts for the lowly and the needy: 'He sets the lowly on high,' Job 5:11, 'He saves the needy from the sword,' Job 5:15. These are attributes the whole Bible confirms, and a reader who dismisses them because Eliphaz said them has lost something.

He speaks of a God who is holy beyond the reach of the creature. The night voice asks whether a mortal can be purer than his Maker, Job 4:17, and says that even God's angels are found wanting, Job 4:18. The point is not that God is harsh but that He is God, and the distance between Creator and creature is real. Isaiah sees the same distance in the temple, Isaiah 6:5. The doctrine of divine holiness is stated here before anyone has applied it wrongly.

He speaks of a God who disciplines those He loves, Job 5:17, and who binds what He wounds, Job 5:18. This is sound, as Hebrews 12:5-6 confirms. It is a picture of a God whose blows are not an end but a means, and whose hands 'also heal.' The trouble is not with the picture but with its fit to Job's case, and the prologue already told us that God Himself named Job blameless and permitted his ruin 'without cause.'

He speaks, in error, of a God who is predictable. Eliphaz's system requires that God's justice can be read off circumstances. The rest of the book, and of Scripture, shows that God's ways are higher than that. The same God who does unsearchable things cannot be searched out by a man's rules, and Job 5:9 and Job 5:27 sit side by side in tension. The passage teaches us that we should not confuse the doctrine of God's justice with the confidence that we can see it operating in each case.

And it shows a God who is silent while people speak on His behalf. In Job 4 and 5 God does not interrupt Eliphaz. He will later say of the friends, 'you have not spoken about Me accurately,' Job 42:7, and it shows a patience with mistaken speech that is itself a mark of His character. He does not stop them and does not need to defend Himself in real time.

For worship, the chapter teaches two things at once. Let the wonders of God, His rain and His rescuing of the lowly, be the material of praise. And be careful with what we say for God to others, since He will hold us to the accuracy of it. A congregation that has learned from Eliphaz will speak boldly of God's power and mercy, and quietly about why He has permitted a particular pain, and will let Him be the one who explains.

crossReferences.note: Job repeats Eliphaz's line from Job 5:9, 'He does great things beyond searching out, and wonders without number,' but uses it to argue that God cannot be brought to court. The same true sentence is used for opposite purposes, which shows how a principle bends to the hand that holds it.

Paul quotes Job 5:13, 'He catches the wise in their craftiness.' It is the New Testament's clearest use of Eliphaz's words, and it shows that a true sentence from a flawed speech can still be Scripture's own voice. Paul applies it to worldly wisdom that thinks it has God worked out.

The letter to the Hebrews quotes Proverbs 3:11-12 to say that the Lord disciplines the one He loves. It gives the truth in Job 5:17 an explicit place in Christian teaching, applied to believers who suffer for Christ, and not as a diagnosis of a particular fault.

'He who sows injustice will reap disaster.' Eliphaz's saying about sowing and reaping in Job 4:8 draws on a real proverb. It shows that his theology has support in wisdom literature, and prepares the reader for the fact that proverbs describe general patterns and not guarantees for each case.

Eliphaz repeats the substance of his night vision in his second speech: 'What is man, that he should be pure?' The return to the same argument shows that his view does not change, and that it grows harsher as Job pushes back.

'He has wounded us, but He will bind up our wounds.' The prophet speaks of a God who tears and heals. It echoes Job 5:18 and shows the pattern as an Israelite conviction, spoken by a people repenting, and not by a sufferer who has done nothing.

Elihu says God speaks in dreams and visions of the night to turn a man from wrongdoing. It offers a scriptural place for visions like Eliphaz's, and also shows that the book does not dismiss them. What it disputes is the use Eliphaz makes of his.

John tells believers not to trust every spirit but to test them. Eliphaz's spirit is never tested, and the verse gives the rule he neglected. It helps readers hold a real experience and a critical judgment together.

The LORD tells Eliphaz that His wrath is kindled against him and his friends because they have not spoken about Him accurately, as Job has. It stands as the final judgment on the speeches, and it teaches readers to read Eliphaz's true words in light of it.

Paul says that no one will be justified by works and that righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ. It gives a New Testament answer to the night voice of Job 4:17, that no mortal is pure before God, and to the question of how a man of clay can stand.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 3 explained why humanity lives in a broken world. Job 4 and 5 show what happens when human wisdom tries to read that brokenness. Eliphaz makes a bold and beautiful attempt: the world has a moral order, and suffering is the mark of a hidden disorder in the sufferer. The attempt has real roots in the Bible, in the curse that follows sin, in Proverbs, in the law's blessings and curses. And it fails at exactly the point where a person, not a principle, is in the room.

The passage looks back to Genesis. The image of man as dust, 'whose foundations are in the dust,' Job 4:19, is Genesis 3:19, 'for dust you are.' The talk of trouble that does not 'spring from the dust' of Job 5:6 echoes the thorns and thistles of the cursed ground. Eliphaz is speaking in the world Genesis 3 made.

It looks forward to the question that the rest of the Bible answers. If no mortal is pure before God, and if the innocent are not spared, what then? The prophets answer with a Servant who bears the sins of many, Isaiah 53:5, and the gospel answers with the Christ who dies, is raised and pours out the Spirit. The wisdom of Eliphaz has no room for a substitute, and that is its ultimate limit.

The passage also prepares the church for its own ministry to sufferers. Eliphaz's mistakes are those of every generation: to preach a principle and forget the person. The New Testament calls us to 'weep with those who weep,' Romans 12:15, and to 'help the weak, be patient with everyone,' 1 Thessalonians 5:14, and the failure of the friends stands as a caution and as a call.

In the new creation Eliphaz's good promises, and more, will be true without qualification. Job 5:19-26 imagines a man secure from famine and sword, at peace with the beasts of the field, with a full household. Isaiah sees the wolf dwelling with the lamb, Isaiah 11:6, and the Revelation sees a city where 'there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4. What Eliphaz offers as a reward for the disciplined is given in the end as a gift to the redeemed, on the ground of a righteousness not their own.

quiz.q: What is the central principle Eliphaz states in 4:7-8?

options.text: That the innocent do not perish, and those who sow trouble reap the same, implying suffering proves guilt.
options.note: This retribution principle drives Eliphaz's whole argument and will recur, hardening, throughout the friends' later speeches.

options.text: That those who plow iniquity and sow trouble will eventually reap what they have sown.
options.note: A true restatement of half the principle, but less complete than the full claim that innocence itself guarantees safety from perishing.

options.text: That only the wicked ever experience prosperity.
options.note: Eliphaz's principle runs the other direction: prosperity for the righteous and calamity for the wicked, not exclusive prosperity for the wicked.

options.text: That suffering is entirely random and unrelated to anyone's conduct.
options.note: This is the opposite of Eliphaz's actual claim, which strongly links conduct and consequence.

quiz.q: What does the mysterious night vision in 4:12-21 declare?

options.text: That no mortal can be more righteous than God, and even His angels are charged with error, so how much less those who dwell in houses of clay.
options.note: The vision's message in verses 17 to 19 makes this universal claim about human and even angelic frailty before God.

options.text: That every human being, being made of dust, falls short of God's purity.
options.note: Captures the vision's basic thrust about human frailty, though less complete than its fuller argument from angels down to mortals.

options.text: That angels are entirely free from any possibility of error.
options.note: The vision says the opposite, that God charges even His angels with error, as part of its argument from greater to lesser.

options.text: That Job specifically has committed a great sin.
options.note: The vision speaks in general terms about mortals and angels; it does not name any specific sin of Job's.

quiz.q: What promise does Eliphaz make in 5:17-27 to the one God disciplines?

options.text: That such a person will be rescued from calamity, secure in their home, blessed with many descendants, and will come to the grave in full vigor.
options.note: This is the sweeping restoration Eliphaz promises, assuming Job's submission to correction will reverse his losses.

options.text: That God wounds but also binds up, so that real healing and blessing eventually follow real discipline.
options.note: A true summary of Eliphaz's wounds-and-binds pattern, though less complete than his full, sweeping list of promised blessings.

options.text: That God's discipline never actually wounds, only heals.
options.note: Eliphaz explicitly says God wounds and also binds, strikes and also heals; the wounding is real, not denied.

options.text: That they will suffer even more severely as further correction.
options.note: Eliphaz promises the opposite outcome, restoration and blessing, not escalating suffering.

quiz.q: Why does the reader have reason to be cautious about Eliphaz's speech, even though much of it sounds true?

options.text: Because the reader already knows from chapters 1 and 2 that Job's suffering was not caused by any sin, so Eliphaz's application of his true general principles to Job's specific case is mistaken.
options.note: This is the central irony the narrator has set up: the reader has information the characters in the dialogue do not.

options.text: Because Eliphaz assumes his general theological principle must explain Job's specific, unique situation.
options.note: Names the real error, though less precise than pointing to the exact information, chapters 1 and 2, that exposes it.

options.text: Because everything Eliphaz says is entirely false.
options.note: Many of his individual statements, such as God's discipline of those He loves, are true in general; the error lies in the application to Job.

options.text: Because Eliphaz is portrayed as speaking in bad faith.
options.note: Nothing in the text suggests Eliphaz is insincere; he appears to genuinely believe his counsel will help Job.

quiz.q: What later verse in the book directly evaluates speeches like Eliphaz's first one?

options.text: Job 42:7, where God tells Eliphaz that he and his two friends have not spoken of God what is right, as His servant Job has.
options.note: This final verdict retroactively marks the friends' application of their theology, including this speech, as mistaken.

options.text: The book's closing chapters, where God addresses Eliphaz and his companions directly about their speeches.
options.note: Points to the right general location, but less precise than citing 42:7 exactly and its specific wording about not speaking rightly.

options.text: Job 5:27, Eliphaz's own closing claim that his words are true.
options.note: This is Eliphaz's own self-assessment within the speech, not an outside verdict on it; the book's actual judgment comes later, from God.

options.text: Job 1:22, describing Job's response to his first losses.
options.note: That verse evaluates Job's own response to suffering, not Eliphaz's later theological speeches.

questions: Eliphaz begins gently, reminding Job of his own past wisdom, before his counsel eventually turns harder to bear. How do you notice the moment when well-meant counsel starts to wound rather than help, in yourself or others?

Much of what Eliphaz says about God, His discipline, His care for the humble, His unsearchable greatness, is true. What true things about God have you heard misapplied to your own suffering or someone else's in a way that hurt rather than healed?

Eliphaz assumes Job's suffering must trace to some fault. Where are you tempted to look for a tidy explanation for pain, yours or another's, rather than sit with the honest possibility that some suffering has no such explanation?

Eliphaz's promise of restoration in 5:17-27 is beautiful and largely true of God's ways in general. How do you hold real hope for God's future goodness without turning it into a demand that He restore things on your own timeline?

God's later rebuke of the friends reminds us that even sincere, doctrinally careful counsel can still be wrong. When you comfort someone who is suffering, what would it look like to hold your own explanations more loosely?

translationNotes.note: The uprightness of your ways your hope reflects Eliphaz's underlying assumption that righteous conduct should function as a guarantee against calamity, an assumption the book as a whole contests.

By the breath of God renders a phrase using eloah, the poetic singular divine name that dominates Job's speeches far more than the covenant name YHWH, common in narrative sections of the Old Testament.
Discipline renders musar, the same key term used throughout Proverbs for corrective, formative instruction; Eliphaz assumes it explains Job's suffering, an assumption God will later correct.
